title: Divisibility By Three OQ-01: General Last-k-Digits, Powers of 2 and 5, and Digital Root Theory
description: A comprehensive extension of divisibility-by-three covering: a general last-k-digit theorem unifying all power-of-2 and power-of-5 divisibility rules; general theorems that 2^k | 10^k and 5^k | 10^k with corollaries 2^k | n ↔ 2^k | (n mod 10^k) and 5^k | n ↔ 5^k | (n mod 10^k); divisibility by 13 via the truncation method; digit sum rules for 37, 99, 999, and 27 via multi-digit groupings; casting out nines and threes theory with addition and multiplication preservation; digital root theory with a full characterization; and coprime factorization rules for 6, 12, 15, 18, 36, 45, 60, and 90.

meta.author: Lean Genius
originalContributions: General dvd_iff_dvd_mod theorem with clean proof via Euclidean division and Nat.dvd_add
pow2_dvd_pow10 and pow5_dvd_pow10 with the general pow2_dvd_last_k and pow5_dvd_last_k corollaries
Divisibility by 13 via truncation (add 4× last digit) proved as an iff theorem
Multi-digit grouping rules: 37, 99, 999, 27 via digitSum_dvd_iff helper
Casting out nines and threes: modEq preservation under addition and multiplication
General digit_sum_add_modEq and digit_sum_mul_modEq for arbitrary (b, d) pairs
Digital root definition with full properties: le_9, zero, pos, eq_9_iff characterization
Coprime factorization rules for 6, 12, 15, 18, 36, 45, 60, 90 as iff theorems

overview.historicalContext: The divisibility-by-three rule (digit sum divisible by 3) is one of the most ancient arithmetic shortcuts, exploiting the congruence 10 ≡ 1 (mod 3). This extension systematically develops the underlying theory: the general principle that d | 10^k enables 'last k digits' tests, and the Mathlib modEq_digits_sum framework handles all digit-sum rules uniformly. Casting out nines is a practical arithmetic verification technique known since medieval times. The digital root function encapsulates the iterative digit-summing process and has applications in recreational mathematics.
overview.problemStatement: Provide a comprehensive formal treatment of divisibility in the natural numbers, covering: (1) a unified general theorem for all last-k-digit rules; (2) infinite families of rules 2^k | n and 5^k | n; (3) the 13-truncation rule; (4) digit-group sum rules for 37, 99, 999, 27; (5) casting out nines and threes with arithmetic preservation; (6) digital root theory; (7) coprime factorization rules for all products of {2, 3, 4, 5, 9} up to 90.
overview.proofStrategy: The dvd_iff_dvd_mod master theorem is proved by Euclidean division: n = M·(n/M) + (n mod M), so if d | M then d | M·(n/M), making d | n equivalent to d | (n mod M). Powers of 2 and 5 divide corresponding powers of 10 by factoring 10 = 2×5. Digit-sum rules use Mathlib's Nat.modEq_digits_sum. The 13-truncation uses IsCoprime (13, 10) to cancel 10 from a linear combination. Digital root characterization uses a case split on whether n mod 9 is 0.
keyInsights: The theorem dvd_iff_dvd_mod subsumes all specific last-k-digit rules: 2 (M=10), 4 (M=100), 8 (M=1000), 5 (M=10), 25 (M=100), 125 (M=1000), 16 (M=10000), 32 (M=100000), and more
The general theorems pow2_dvd_last_k and pow5_dvd_last_k capture infinite families of divisibility rules in single universally quantified statements
Casting out nines for multiplication (casting_out_nines_mul) is the theoretical basis for the schoolroom error-detection technique: digit sums multiply mod 9
The digital root is completely characterized by: digitalRoot n = 9 iff 9 | n (for n > 0); otherwise digitalRoot n = n mod 9
The coprime factorization theorems generalize to composite rules: 6 = 2×3, 12 = 4×3, 15 = 3×5, 18 = 2×9, 36 = 4×9, 45 = 5×9, 60 = 4×3×5, 90 = 2×9×5

conclusion.summary: This 550-line, 56-theorem formalization provides the most comprehensive treatment of elementary divisibility rules in the gallery. It establishes the theoretical foundations (general last-k-digit theorem, power families, digit-sum framework) and applies them to a wide range of specific divisors, including all commonly tested divisors up to 125 and coprime products up to 90.
conclusion.implications: The unified dvd_iff_dvd_mod theorem shows that an infinite family of divisibility rules (one for each pair (d, M) with d | M) are all corollaries of a single modular arithmetic fact. The casting out nines module demonstrates that digit-sum residues are preserved under ring operations, explaining why the technique correctly detects arithmetic errors.
openQuestions: Extend to an automated tactic that generates and verifies divisibility rules for arbitrary input divisors d coprime to a given base b
Formalize the convergence of the digital root iteration: starting from any n, repeated digit-summing always terminates at digitalRoot n in finitely many steps
Generalize casting out nines to arbitrary moduli: digit-sum mod d is preserved under addition and multiplication whenever b ≡ 1 (mod d)

sections.title: Part I: General Last-k-Digits Theorem
sections.summary: Establishes dvd_iff_dvd_mod — the master theorem unifying all last-k-digit divisibility rules. If d | M, then d | n iff d | (n mod M). Every specific rule (2 via M=10, 4 via M=100, 5 via M=10, 25 via M=100, etc.) is a one-line corollary. The proof uses Euclidean division n = M·(n/M) + (n mod M) and Nat.dvd_add.

sections.title: Part II: Infinite Power Families (2^k and 5^k)
sections.summary: Proves pow2_dvd_pow10 and pow5_dvd_pow10 (both 2^k | 10^k and 5^k | 10^k), then applies dvd_iff_dvd_mod to get the universally quantified pow2_dvd_last_k and pow5_dvd_last_k: for all k and n, 2^k | n iff 2^k | (n mod 10^k), and similarly for 5^k. One theorem simultaneously covers all rules for 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 5, 25, 125.

sections.title: Part III: Divisibility by 13 — Truncation Method
sections.summary: Proves thirteen_dvd_truncation: 13 | n iff 13 | (n/10 + 4·(n%10)). The algebraic key is 10(q + 4r) = n + 39r where n = 10q + r, so 13 | 10(q+4r) iff 13 | n. IsCoprime (13, 10) cancels the 10 factor: gcd(13,10) = 1 implies 13 | 10·x → 13 | x. The proof works over ℤ to handle signed subtraction cleanly.

sections.title: Part IV: Digit-Sum Rules via Mathlib
sections.summary: Introduces digitSum_dvd_iff (d | n iff d | (digits b n).sum when b ≡ 1 mod d) using Nat.modEq_digits_sum. Applies to: 3 and 9 (base 10), 37 (base 1000 since 1000 ≡ 1 mod 37), 99 (base 100), 999 (base 1000), 27 (base 1000 since 27 | 999), and 7 in base 8 (8 ≡ 1 mod 7). Each rule collapses to a one-line native_decide verification of the base congruence.

sections.title: Part V: Casting Out Nines and Threes
sections.summary: Establishes casting_out_nines_add and casting_out_nines_mul: digit sums are preserved modulo 9 (and 3) under addition and multiplication. The general digit_sum_add_modEq and digit_sum_mul_modEq work for any base b and any d with b ≡ 1 (mod d). This formalizes the schoolroom error-detection technique: if digit_sum(a × b) ≢ digit_sum(a) × digit_sum(b) (mod 9), the multiplication is wrong.

sections.title: Part VI: Digital Root Theory
sections.summary: Defines digitalRoot n (0 if n=0; 9 if n>0 and 9|n; n mod 9 otherwise) and proves its complete characterization: digitalRoot_le_9, digitalRoot_zero, digitalRoot_pos, digitalRoot_eq_9_iff (9 | n ↔ digitalRoot n = 9), and digitalRoot_mod3 (3 | n ↔ 3 | digitalRoot n). The implementation captures the fixed point of the digit-summing iteration without needing well-founded recursion.

sections.title: Part VII: Composite Rules via Coprime Factorization
sections.summary: Proves coprime_mul_dvd_iff: if gcd(d₁, d₂) = 1 then d₁ × d₂ | n iff d₁ | n and d₂ | n. Applies this via native_decide coprimality checks to give iff rules for 6=2×3, 12=4×3, 15=3×5, 18=2×9, 36=4×9, 45=5×9, 60=4×15, 90=9×10. Nat.Coprime.mul_dvd_of_dvd_of_dvd is the Mathlib tool for the Chinese Remainder direction.

sections.title: Part VIII: Truncation Methods for 7 and 11
sections.summary: Extends the truncation method beyond 13 to divisibility by 7 and 11. For 7: the osculator is −2 (subtract 2× last digit), proved via 10q + r → 7 | q − 2r iff 7 | 10q + r using IsCoprime (7, 10). For 11: the alternating digit sum rule uses 10 ≡ −1 (mod 11), so digits contribute with alternating ±1 weights. Includes combined rules using coprime factorization for products involving 7, such as 14, 21, and 77.
